name: Cognitive Bias
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why Smart People Buy the Top: Cognitive Bias and Blockchain Hype
lesson.summary: A cognitive bias is a systematic, predictable pattern in how people misjudge information, and recognizing the specific biases that blockchain hype and blockchain skepticism both exploit is a basic skill needed before evaluating any of the cost or architecture claims covered in this book.
lesson.body:
A cognitive bias is a systematic pattern of deviation from careful, rational judgment, a kind of mental shortcut that usually saves time and works fine in ordinary life but predictably misleads people in specific, well documented situations. It is worth being precise about what this is not: a cognitive bias is not a sign of low intelligence or a lack of information. Careful, well informed, highly educated people fall into these same patterns constantly, because the patterns come from how human judgment works in general, not from any particular person's shortcomings.

A handful of biases show up again and again around blockchain projects, and it helps to know them by name. Herd behavior, sometimes described with the acronym FOMO, fear of missing out, pushes people to buy into something mainly because everyone around them seems to be buying into it, treating the crowd's enthusiasm as evidence rather than checking the evidence directly. Confirmation bias leads someone who has already decided a project is promising to notice and remember every piece of supporting news while quietly discounting or forgetting anything that contradicts that belief. The sunk cost fallacy keeps people holding onto a losing position specifically because they have already put money or time into it, as though spending more now could somehow retroactively make the earlier spending worthwhile, when in fact past spending has no bearing on whether continuing is currently a good idea. Authority bias leads people to trust a claim more because a celebrity, an influencer, or someone who simply sounds confident endorsed it, rather than because the claim itself holds up.

Survivorship bias deserves particular attention here because of how quietly it distorts everyday conversation. Someone who bought an early position in a successful project and made money talks about it openly, at parties, online, to friends. Someone who bought into a project that failed usually goes quiet, because admitting a loss is uncomfortable in a way that celebrating a win is not. The result is that the stories reaching any given person skew heavily toward success, not because success was actually typical, but because success is simply the outcome people are willing to talk about. Anyone forming an impression of "how people generally do" here from overheard conversations is working from a badly distorted sample without realizing it.

Recognizing these patterns is not just useful for someone deciding whether to buy a token. It is a prerequisite skill for reading the rest of this book carefully, because both blockchain promoters and blockchain skeptics can trigger the exact same biases toward opposite conclusions. A breathless claim that a new chain will change everything leans on herd behavior and authority bias just as surely as a dismissive claim that the whole technology is worthless can lean on confirmation bias in a reader who already wants to hear that. Neither kind of claim becomes true or false because of how persuasively it is delivered.

The practical habit worth building, and the one this book will keep returning to, is to pause and ask what specific evidence would change your mind before accepting a claim, and to actively look for the base rate, how these kinds of projects have generally turned out, rather than relying on whichever anecdotes happen to be loudest. That habit is what makes it possible to sit down with the cost figures and architecture tradeoffs covered throughout the rest of this book and evaluate them on their merits, rather than on how good or bad they make you feel.
